title: Cross-Border Counsel: Decoding The 2025 Amendment To The Bar Council Rules On Practice By Foreign Law Firms & Lawyers In India
pub: LiveLaw (Law Firm Articles) — authors at Dua Associates
author: Angad Varma · Agastya Sen

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses India’s regulation of foreign lawyers and law firms, not legal AI capability, verification, selective deployment or operating-model redesign. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine a position on the cluster’s proposition.

mo.t: Global legal markets: Liberalization remains locally contested
Legal outsourcing: Commercial growth need not advance workers
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs
Public justice: AI access requires accountable adjudication
Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production

kp.k: Foreign legal market opening remains grounded in reciprocity
kp.d: This practitioner article addresses cross-border legal-market regulation rather than AI. The authors describe the rules notified in March 2023 as opening non-litigious foreign and international legal practice to foreign lawyers and firms. They attribute the amendment notified on 13th May, 2025 to opposition from Indian lawyers, firms and State Bar Councils, and argue that it effectively replaces the earlier rules while retaining reciprocity.
qs: The 2022 Rules opened the door for foreign lawyers and foreign law firms to practice foreign and international laws in India in non-litigious matters including legal advisory, corporate transactions and international commercial arbitration.
The 2025 Amendment provides clarity on the scope of the 2022 Rules without derogating from the fundamental principle enshrined therein: reciprocity.

kp.k: Judicial intervention preceded regulated foreign entry
kp.d: The authors report that the BCI initially opposed foreign entry and challenged the Madras High Court's permission for fly-in, fly-out advice and international commercial arbitration appearances. They describe the Supreme Court's judgment dated 13th March, 2018 as narrowing that permission while allowing the BCI to frame entry rules.
qs: The BCI initially opposed the entry of foreign lawyers and foreign law firms into India in any form.

by its judgment dated 13th March, 2018 diluted the blanket permission granted by the Madras High Court, while providing BCI the liberty to frame appropriate rules on the entry of foreign lawyers and law firms in India.

kp.k: Foreign entry preserves boundaries around Indian legal practice
kp.d: The article describes the 2022 framework as permitting registered foreign providers to advise on foreign or international law in transactional matters, participate in specified international commercial arbitrations and establish offices reciprocally. It distinguishes these permissions from prohibitions on Indian-law advice, domestic litigation and work requiring Indian enrolment.
qs: Setting up of offices in India on a reciprocal basis.

Consequently, the 2022 Rules prohibited foreign lawyers and foreign law firms, whether registered with the BCI or not, from undertaking inter alia any of the following activities: advising clients on Indian law; appearing before courts, tribunals, or statutory authorities in India; engaging in litigation practice; or undertaking any other work that requires enrolment with the BCI or a State Bar Council.

kp.k: Amendment narrows foreign participation in Indian-seated arbitrations
kp.d: According to the authors, the amendment permits foreign lawyers and firms to represent clients whose principal office is abroad in international arbitrations in India only when the issues concern foreign law, international law or both. They explicitly contrast this with the 2022 permission, which did not require foreign law to be involved.
qs: Foreign lawyers and law firms are permitted to represent clients, having their principal office is in a foreign country, in international arbitrations in India, when the issue(s) involved are limited to foreign law, international law or a combination thereof.
It bears emphasis that the 2022 Rules permitted foreign lawyers and law firms to appear in international commercial arbitration proceedings in India, regardless of whether foreign law was involved.

kp.k: Temporary practice faces detailed presence and disclosure conditions
kp.d: The article reports that unregistered fly-in, fly-out practice is limited to foreign-law, home-system or international advice, with engagements originating inside or outside India. Providers cannot maintain offices, infrastructure or a regular presence. The authors state a limit of 60 consecutive calendar days within any 12-month period, counted from initial arrival regardless of exits and re-entries. They also describe a Form C declaration, BCI resolution of scope disputes and applicable ethical requirements unless exempted.
qs: they must not establish any office, infrastructure, or maintain a regular presence in India
their cumulative presence must not exceed 60 consecutive calendar days within any 12-month period, counted from the initial date of arrival, irrespective of any exits and re-entries

they must submit a declaration in Form C (under the 2022 Rules) detailing the nature of work, areas of law, client particulars, jurisdictions involved, and a confirmation that Indian law will not be practiced

kp.k: Partnerships and referrals receive different registration treatment
kp.d: The authors distinguish formal partnerships, requiring registration of all parties under the 2022 Rules, from referrals and consultancy or advisory engagement contracts, which do not require the Indian participant to register. They regard this as greater specificity than the earlier allowance for informal collaboration.
qs: Partnerships between foreign lawyers and law firms, and Indian lawyers and law firms are permitted only when all parties are registered under the 2022 Rules.
However, for referral arrangements or engagement contracts for consultancy and advisory, would not require the Indian lawyer and law firm to be registered under the 2022 Rules.

kp.k: Indian lawyers retain conditional domestic court appearance rights
kp.d: The article contrasts the earlier restriction of Indian-enrolled partners and associates in foreign firms to non-litigious foreign or international-law work with the amendment's conditional permission for Indian court and tribunal appearances. Such appearances must involve matters referred by their foreign firms, rather than practice through those firms.
qs: In a deviation from the 2022 Rules on the permitted activities of Indian enrolled Partners and Associates in foreign law firms, the 2025 Amendment clarifies that such Partners and Associates may appear in Indian courts and tribunals only when such matters are referred to them by their respective foreign law firms, and not when practising through foreign law firms.

kp.k: Definitional clarity accompanies stricter registration compliance
kp.d: The authors report new definitions differentiating foreign lawyers, Indian advocates, Indian advocates seeking foreign-lawyer registration, foreign firms, Indian firms and Indian-foreign firms. Alongside this clarification, they describe more demanding documentation, declarations and recurring compliance obligations.
qs: Clear definitions of relevant terms, including: (a) 'Foreign Lawyer'; (b) 'Indian Advocate/Lawyer'; (c) 'Indian Advocate/Lawyer who seeks registration as a foreign lawyer'; (d) 'Foreign Law Firm'; (e) 'Indian Law Firm'; (f) 'Indian-Foreign Law Firm'.

The 2025 Amendment also introduces stricter procedural prerequisites for registration, through a detailed, comprehensive and exhaustive registration process comprising of numerous documentary requirements, declarations and recurring compliances.

kp.k: Professional obligations frame the balance between openness and protection
kp.d: The authors present Indian legal practice as fiduciary and ethical rather than commercial, regulated by the BCI under the Advocates Act, 1961. They characterize the amendment as balancing foreign market access with protection of Indian lawyers and firms, and as enabling collaboration without sacrificing existing statutory rights. This is their interpretation of the regulatory design, not a measured outcome.
qs: The legal profession in India is not treated as a commercial activity or a contract of service.
The legal field is rooted in fiduciary and ethical responsibilities, aimed at ensuring equal access of justice.

The 2025 Amendment is a step forward in the same direction, striking a balance between offering foreign law firms and lawyers' access to markets in India, whilst protecting and safeguarding the interests of Indian law firms and lawyers.

kp.k: Economic integration supports anticipated cross-border legal demand
kp.d: The authors expect legal-services demand to surge with economic growth and international integration. They cite S&P Global Inc.'s projection of India becoming the third-largest economy by 2030 with GDP of USD 7.3 trillion, and identify the UK Free Trade Agreement and other bilateral pacts as demand drivers. Separately, they report the BCI's belief that limited opening will benefit Indian lawyers and meet service demand; neither benefit is established through outcome evidence here.
qs: India is currently the fourth largest economy and is poised to become the third largest by 2030 with a projected GDP of USD 7.3 trillion as per S&P Global Inc., consequently the demand for legal services is expected to surge.
The UK Free Trade Agreement, alongside other bilateral trade pacts, underscores India's integration with foreign jurisdictions and amplifies the need for foreign lawyers and law firms.

The BCI believes that opening the legal profession in India to foreign lawyers, limited to the practice of foreign law, handling internal legal non-litigious matters and participating in international arbitrations will ultimately benefit Indian lawyers and serve the demand for such services.

kp.k: Compliance and litigation may delay foreign participation
kp.d: The authors predict an initial wait-and-watch response because of extensive compliance and judicial uncertainty. They identify Narendra Sharma & Ors. v. Bar Council of India & Ors., WP (C) No. 1556 of 2024, as a pending Delhi High Court challenge to the 2022 Rules that does not restrain their operation. Their expectation of fresh challenges to the amendment is expressly speculative, based on continued opposition from lawyer associations.
qs: Nonetheless, the exhaustive compliance requirements, coupled with pending judicial challenges, may initially hinder participation of foreign law firms and lawyers who may follow a wait and watch approach.
which although remains pending, does not restrain the operation of the 2022 Rules.
Also, given the consistent resistance adopted by various associations of lawyers across the country, we anticipate that there may be fresh judicial challenges against the 2025 Amendment.

kp.k: Limited initial entry contrasts with optimistic participation forecasts
kp.d: The article reports that only three foreign law firms had entered India as of April 2025, describing the response to the earlier, partly ambiguous rules as lukewarm. The authors predict that reciprocity, definitional clarity and broader permissible activities will make India more attractive and increase participation as uncertainties diminish. This is a forward-looking assessment qualified by their discussion of stringent conditions and possible delays.
qs: The response to the 2022 Rules which were ambiguous in parts has so far been lukewarm, with only three foreign law firms having entered India as of April 2025.
The 2025 Amendment is expected to attract greater participation by removal of procedural and legal uncertainties.

While the stringent conditions of the 2025 Amendment may seem as an initial hurdle, there is optimism that as the dust settles, more foreign lawyers and law firms will look to enter and participate in permissible legal activities in India.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article makes no AI claims. In its own domain, Varma and Sen predict that India's economic growth and international integration will increase legal-services demand, while regulatory clarification will encourage foreign-firm participation and collaboration with Indian lawyers.
pts.d: The authors describe the 2025 Amendment as balancing foreign access with protection for Indian practitioners. They argue that it clarifies permissible activities and creates collaboration opportunities, although the arbitration permission is narrower than under the earlier rules. They predict greater participation as legal uncertainty diminishes, but also anticipate initial hesitation because of compliance burdens and litigation, and possible fresh judicial challenges. Their presentation of the BCI's belief that opening the profession will benefit Indian lawyers is a reported regulatory rationale, rather than independent evidence of that benefit.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support their outlook with regulatory interpretation, a reported entry count, an attributed economic projection, trade integration and pending litigation—not measured post-amendment outcomes.
pts.d: The article compares the 2022 Rules with the amendment notified on 13 May 2025, covering arbitration, fly-in/fly-out practice, partnerships, referrals and registration. It reports that only three foreign firms had entered India by April 2025, without identifying a source for that count. It attributes the 2030 GDP projection to S&P Global and invokes the UK Free Trade Agreement and other bilateral pacts as demand drivers. The pending Delhi High Court challenge and opposition by lawyers' associations underpin the prediction of near-term hesitation. No quantified forecast of legal demand or future foreign-firm entry is provided.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The outlook distinguishes initial compliance-related hesitation from unspecified later growth in participation; access remains conditional on reciprocity and restricted practice permissions.
pts.d: Writing on 27 May 2025, the authors use April 2025 entry figures as a baseline and a 2030 economic projection as demand context. They give no date for increased foreign participation. As they describe the rules, foreign practice remains limited to permitted foreign/international-law activities; arbitration representation requires a foreign-principal-office client and issues limited to foreign law, international law or both. Partnerships require all parties to register under the rules, whereas referral or consultancy arrangements do not require Indian practitioners to register. Fly-in/fly-out access carries presence, declaration and no-office conditions. These are qualifications to market opening, not predictions of unrestricted entry.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are foreign firms seeking Indian market access, Indian practitioners seeking collaboration, and businesses needing cross-border legal advice.
pts.d: Foreign lawyers and firms gain clearer routes to permitted work but face extensive compliance and scope restrictions. Indian firms and lawyers gain partnership and referral opportunities while retaining protected domestic-practice rights. The authors describe a specific change for Indian-enrolled partners and associates of foreign firms: court and tribunal appearances are permitted on referrals from those firms, but not through the foreign firms. Internationally active clients and businesses are presented as the source of demand for a more open framework. The article does not predict AI-related effects on staffing, fees or access to justice.
